text: Giordano worked so fast that people nicknamed him Luca fa presto, which means Luca paints quickly. He trained with Ribera around 1650. His father Antonio was a painter, and Ribera's half length philosophers shaped Giordano, who painted many of them himself. Around 1652 he went to Rome for the first time and studied the Baroque art of Pietro da Cortona. He also earned the names The Thunderbolt and The Proteus of painting, since he could imitate other painters so well. Later he worked in Naples, Rome, Florence and Venice before ten years in Spain.

Italians nicknamed Honthorst Gherardo delle Notti, or Gerard of the Nights, for his scenes lit by artificial light. He was born in Utrecht, trained with his father, a decorative painter, and then with Abraham Bloemaert. In Rome he lodged at the palace of Vincenzo Giustiniani, where he painted Christ Before the High Priest. Cardinal Scipione Borghese became another patron. He came back to Utrecht in 1620. Queen Elizabeth of Bohemia, living in exile in the Netherlands, employed him as a painter and as a drawing master for her children, and through her Charles I invited him to England in 1628.

The Royal Danish Academy in Copenhagen turned Tidemand away at first. He studied at a private art school and soon became a pupil at the academy anyway. From 1837 he studied in Düsseldorf under Theodor Hildebrandt. In Hardanger he met the 18 year old Hans Gude, and the two became close friends who made landscape paintings together, with Tidemand adding the figures. He travelled around Norway to study folk costumes, tools and buildings. In 1848 King Oscar I asked him to paint a series of Norwegian peasant life for the palace of Oscarshall.

Macke lived most of his creative life in Bonn, with short stays at Lake Thun and trips to Paris, Italy, the Netherlands and Tunisia. His father was a building contractor and amateur artist, and his drawings were the first art to impress the boy. Macke enrolled at the Kunstakademie Düsseldorf in 1904, the year his father died. In Paris in 1907 he saw the Impressionists, and soon afterwards he spent a few months in Lovis Corinth's studio in Berlin. Through his friend Franz Marc he met Kandinsky. He died in the First World War.

Hackert's pictures of the Battle of Chesma were made for Catherine the Great, and some of his battle scenes hang in the Peterhof palace in Russia. He grew up in Prenzlau in Brandenburg, trained with his father, a portraitist and animal painter, and went to the Prussian Academy in Berlin. In Paris he worked mostly in gouache. He left for Italy in 1768 and settled mainly in Rome and Naples, where he produced many works for Sir William Hamilton. Goethe became his friend when he visited Naples in 1786. Goethe also wrote the first biography of Hackert.

Isabey drew himself and his family in a picture called Boat, and it was a success at the Salon of 1820. At 19 he became a pupil of Jacques-Louis David after lessons from the miniature painter François Dumont. He painted the dukes of Angoulême and Berry for the Palace of Versailles. Josephine and Napoleon Bonaparte both backed him, and he planned the ceremonies for their coronation and prepared drawings for the book that recorded it. Several rulers gave him commissions until his death in 1855. His son Eugène painted seascapes.

König made more than 100 transparent paintings, and he showed them by candlelight to paying audiences. He started in his father's trade as a decorative painter in Bern, then studied with Marquard Wocher and Sigmund Freudenberger and learned printmaking from Balthasar Anton Dunker. In 1797 the family left Bern for the Bernese Oberland, where he made coloured etchings, lithographs and small oil paintings for visitors. His costume pictures and scenes of country life came out as popular print series. In 1811 he began showing his Diaphanorama in Bern. Later he toured with it.

De Zwart's father painted carriages, and at 14 the boy was apprenticed to a carriage maker to learn the same trade. In his spare time he copied prints from magazines, and a year later he joined the evening class at the Royal Academy in The Hague. Maris took him into his studio. Jacob Maris once sent him to the coast without drawing materials and made him paint his impressions straight onto canvas when he got back. At the Mauritshuis he copied Vermeer, Potter and Rembrandt. People call him the Hague Breitner for his likeness to George Hendrik Breitner.

Hodges first made a living by painting theatre scenery, after he studied under William Shipley and in the studio of Richard Wilson. Between 1772 and 1775 he sailed with James Cook as the expedition's artist. The big oil paintings from that trip were finished in London, where the Admiralty paid him a salary to complete them. Critics complained that his strong light and colour contrasts made the pictures look rough and unfinished. In 1780 he went to India under the patronage of Warren Hastings. His Benares sketches later became the base for The Ghauts at Benares.

Houbraken says Visscher was an able etcher who had an unusual talent for drawing live models in charcoal. He was born and died in Haarlem, and he trained with Pieter Claesz Soutman. His prints copied painters from Haarlem such as Nicolaes Berchem, Adriaen van Ostade, Pieter van Laer and Adriaen Brouwer. He also made a series of portraits of religious figures from Amsterdam and Haarlem. In 1653 he joined the Haarlem Guild of St. Luke. His work influenced Dirk Helmbreker and Cornelis Bega.

Cort lived his last twelve years in Italy, where people called him Cornelio Fiammingo. He came from Hoorn or Edam, and his first known engravings came out in Antwerp around 1553, published by Hieronymus Cock. In 1565 he moved to Venice and lived in the house of Titian, and he engraved many of Titian's works. Later he went on to Bologna and Rome, and in Rome he founded a school of engraving. He may also have worked for the Medici in Florence. He is said to have engraved upwards of 151 plates.

Isabey wanted to be a sailor, but his father insisted that he study painting. After lessons with his father and copying at the Louvre, he shared a studio at Honfleur with the landscape painter Xavier Leprince in 1824. In 1831 he turned down a place on a diplomatic mission to Morocco, so his friend Delacroix went instead. Isabey became a court painter to King Louis-Philippe, and he painted the return of Napoleon's remains aboard the Belle Poule. He also painted many storms and shipwrecks. His students included Eugène Boudin and Johan Barthold Jongkind.

Verneuil took his ideas from Japanese art and from nature, especially the sea. He learned his trade from the Swiss designer Eugène Grasset. His bold floral designs went onto ceramic tiles, wallpapers and furnishing textiles, and he also made posters in France alongside artists such as Toulouse-Lautrec and Chéret. After the First World War he moved to Geneva. In 1923 he set off with his wife Adélaïde Verneuil de Marval, who was also a painter, on a long voyage to the Far East. He trained many artists, among them Amédée Ozenfant.

Mortimer's father was a customs officer who also dealt in flour and owned several mills. By 1757 the son was studying in London at the Duke of Richmond's Academy, where he became friends with Joseph Wright. In 1759 he won a first prize for a study after Michelangelo's Bacchus. The Society of Artists gave him prizes for paintings of British history, and he became its president in 1774. He painted the figures for several of Thomas Jones's landscapes. He died at 39.

Modersohn-Becker painted many self-portraits, some of them nudes. She grew up in Dresden as the third of seven children, and her father worked as an engineer for the German railway. In 1888 the family moved to Bremen. She is recognised as the first known woman painter to paint nude self-portraits, and she is believed to be the first woman artist to show herself pregnant. A museum devoted only to her work opened in 1927. She died at 31.

Decamps showed everyday life in the East to Paris at the Salon of 1831. In his youth he travelled there and painted Oriental life and scenery with a bold truth to nature that puzzled conventional critics. Before long he was ranked with Delacroix and Ingres as one of the leaders of the French school. His brushstrokes were bold and sometimes rough, and his colour and light had startling contrasts. He also painted Bible scenes against a true local background. He loved dogs and field sports, and in 1860 he died after a fall from a horse while hunting at Fontainebleau.

Chodowiecki made several thousand etchings, mostly small ones, and they show the life of the middle classes in great detail. He grew up in Danzig, and when his father died he and his brother went to live with an uncle in Berlin. Daniel was 16. In Augsburg a painter named Haid gave him his art training. He was admitted to the Berlin Academy in 1764 and became its director in 1797. Much of his work was illustrating books, among them scientific books by Basedow, Buffon, Lavater and Pestalozzi. He died in 1801.

Burger and his old friend Jakob Fürchtegott Dielmann founded the Kronberg Artists' Colony in 1861, and he stayed there until he died. People called him the King of Kronberg. He had studied at the Städelschule in Frankfurt, where Philipp Veit told him to go to Munich. A study trip to Paris brought him together with Corot and Courbet. After he moved to Kronberg, a visit to Antwerp and Amsterdam left him deeply influenced by the Old Masters. In the region around Kronberg, owning a Burger showed good taste.

Dawe painted 329 portraits of Russian generals who fought during Napoleon's invasion, for the Military Gallery of the Winter Palace. He moved to Saint Petersburg in 1819. Pushkin wrote friendly verses about him. His father Philip was a mezzotint engraver, and George first trained with him as an engraver before he turned to painting and won the gold medal of the Royal Academy Schools in 1803. He carried out dissections in his own home to understand the human body better. Classical pictures made his early name, but he cared more about money and went after portrait commissions.

Boys was articled to the engraver George Cooke. When that ended he went to Paris, where Richard Parkes Bonington talked him out of engraving and into painting. William Callow later shared a studio with him there. He stayed in Paris until 1837 and then went home to lithograph the works of David Roberts and Clarkson Stanfield. His collection of colour lithographs, Picturesque Architecture in Paris, Ghent, Antwerp, Rouen, etc., appeared in 1839, and King Louis-Philippe sent him a ring. He also etched some plates for John Ruskin's Stones of Venice.

Gottlob's 1900 poster for the second exhibition of painter lithographers on the Rue Drouot in Paris shows a strong influence of Toulouse-Lautrec. He studied under the painter and decorator Armand Jobbé-Duval, and his work began to appear in the official salons in 1891. His caricatures ran in Le Rire, Le Sourire and other humorous magazines. In 1904 he joined the Cornet Society, and he designed twelve menus for it. Besides prints and portraits, he painted cityscapes of Paris and landscapes of Normandy and Brittany.

Goodwin & Company began as E. Goodwin and Brother, a New York tobacco firm founded before the American Civil War. Its cigarette brands were Gypsy Queen and Old Judge. In 1887 it was among the first to issue trading cards to promote its brands, at first as sepia photographic prints. Its Old Judge set, made from 1887 to 1890, held over 2,000 images and was the first major set of baseball cards. The 1888 Goodwin Champions set showed 50 athletes. It was the firm's first set printed in colour. The firm then merged into James Buchanan Duke's American Tobacco Company.

Forbes studied under Arthur Fitzwilliam Tait and started out as an animal and landscape painter. During the Civil War he was a special artist for Frank Leslie's Magazine, and he drew detailed, dramatic sketches of soldiers and battles. General Sherman later gave many of his etchings to the government, and they are kept in the War Office at Washington. After the war Forbes painted landscapes and cattle scenes. In 1877 he became an honorary member of the London Etching Club. He died in Brooklyn.

Krøyer was raised in Copenhagen by his aunt and her husband, the zoologist Henrik Nikolai Krøyer, after his mother was judged unfit to care for him. He showed talent at nine and enrolled at the Royal Danish Academy at twelve. In 1874 Heinrich Hirschsprung bought four of his watercolours of fishermen, and that began a lifelong friendship and patronage. Three years later a travel scholarship took him around Europe for years. In Paris he studied under Léon Bonnat and came under the influence of Impressionists such as Monet and Degas. He was one of the Skagen Painters.

Díaz lost his leg as a boy, after a reptile bit his foot in a wood near Sèvres, and the wooden stump that replaced it became famous. He was an orphan at ten. At fifteen he entered the studios at Sèvres, where he decorated porcelain before he turned to painting. Around 1831 he met Théodore Rousseau at Fontainebleau and admired him. Once he followed Rousseau into the forest on his wooden leg to watch how he worked, and in the end Rousseau taught him everything he knew. In 1851 Díaz became a Chevalier of the Légion d'honneur.

Moras was called a Berlin painter all his life, yet he scarcely painted in Berlin itself. He trained in the Berlin studio of the landscape painter Hermann Eschke, and in 1876 he held his first exhibition at the Prussian Academy of Arts. On Eschke's advice he painted in Mecklenburg and on the island of Rügen. Many of his pictures came from rural Brandenburg and later the Spreewald. His style was realistic, with a touch of melancholy. He became known for winter landscapes and for large autumn scenes in warm colours. His son Bruno also became a painter.

Haskell expected to go to Yale on a football scholarship, but his drawing caught people's eye and led to an offer of work in magazine illustration. He ended up in the art department of the New York American. He mostly taught himself, and over the next ten years he made three long trips to Paris. He joined the Académie Julian but did not stay. For a time he was a protege and friend of Whistler, who taught him to etch. He also made posters for magazines such as Scribner's and Collier's. In the First World War the army asked him to develop camouflage.

Van der Borcht brought a new subject into northern art, the monkey scene, also called a singerie. He came from Mechelen, and by 1564 he was working from there for the Antwerp printer Christopher Plantin. He made the drawings for the engravings in many scientific books, including those of Rembert Dodoens and Carolus Clusius. In 1572 Spanish troops sacked Mechelen, and the family fled to Antwerp with almost nothing. Plantin took them in. Van der Borcht stayed in Antwerp as Plantin's full time assistant and illustrated many liturgical books for the Spanish market.

Cicéri came from an artistic family. His father was the stage designer Pierre-Luc-Charles Cicéri, his grandfather was the painter Jean-Baptiste Isabey, and his uncle was Eugène Isabey. He got his first lessons from his father and his uncle. He was one of the first artists to work in Bourron-Marlotte, where he settled in 1849. Two years later he showed at the Salon for the first time. He also published albums of lithographs based on photographs, among them views of the Pyrenees, Switzerland and Savoy. Like his father, he designed theatre sets.

Puvis de Chavannes was born Pierre-Cécile Puvis, the son of a mining engineer, and he added the old family name de Chavannes later. He meant to follow his father's profession until a serious illness stopped his studies. After a trip to Italy he told his family in 1846 that he would be a painter. He studied briefly under Delacroix, who soon closed his studio, and then under Henri Scheffer and Thomas Couture. He preferred to work alone, and his training was not classical. Zola described his work as an art made of reason, passion and will.

In 1894 Picabia copied a collection of Spanish paintings that belonged to his grandfather, swapped the copies for the originals and sold the originals to pay for his stamp collection. His mother died of tuberculosis when he was five, and his father raised him. Three years after the swindle he eloped to Switzerland with one of his mistresses. He tried Impressionism and Pointillism, then Cubism, and he became an early figure of Dada in the United States and France. He denounced Dada in 1921. Later he was briefly linked with Surrealism.

Waldmüller attended the Academy of Fine Arts in Vienna from 1807. In 1814 he married the singer Katharina Weidner and went on tour with her as a set designer. Back in Vienna, he copied old masters and painted portraits, among them one of Beethoven in 1823. Later he turned to landscapes, painted with loving attention to detail, because he believed the close study of nature should be the base of painting. That brought him into disputes with the academy. He was forced to retire in 1857, and Vienna took him back by 1863.

Modersohn made his first visit to Worpswede in July 1889 with Fritz Mackensen, and other students from Düsseldorf followed. In 1895 the group held its first show at the Kunsthalle Bremen, and critics mostly panned it. His first wife died after a long illness, and in 1901 he married Paula Becker, who was also a painter. She died in 1907 of an embolism, shortly after the birth of their daughter. He then moved to nearby Fischerhude. He was the only Worpswede artist to support the Kunsthalle Bremen when it bought Van Gogh's Field with Poppies.

Rousseau was known as le grand refusé, the great refused one, because the Salon jury kept turning him down. In 1836 his large Paysage du Jura was rejected. Eight more works sent between 1836 and 1841 were refused too. After that he sent nothing until 1849, when all three of his entries were accepted. His friend, the critic Théophile Thoré, spoke up for him in the press. His father first regretted that he gave up business for painting, but later backed him in every fight with the Salon.

Vorsterman joined the workshop of Rubens around 1618 and soon became his only engraver. In 1621 a violent dispute broke out, and Rubens's lawyers asked the authorities for a protection order. The cause is not known, but most think it was a fight over who owned the rights to the prints, although Rubens had been godfather to his eldest son. In 1624 Vorsterman went to England and lived on the support of royalty and nobles. Back in Antwerp, he engraved twenty-two of the eighty plates for Van Dyck's Iconography. Old age brought blindness and poverty.

Smits paid 2,000 Belgian francs for a small farm in Achterbos near Mol and built it up into his Malvinahof. He was born in Rotterdam, the son of a decorator, and later studied in Brussels and Munich. A friendship with the painter Albert Neuhuys led to trips together to Drenthe and the Campine in Belgium. The Campine landscape moved him, and in 1888 he settled in Achterbos for good. He lived in poverty there. In 1901 he held his first one man show in Antwerp, and critics praised it, but he found no buyers.

Koryūsai started out as a samurai in the service of the Tsuchiya clan. When the head of the clan died, he became a masterless rōnin and moved to Edo, where he settled near Ryōgoku Bridge. In 1769 he became a print designer under the art name Haruhiro, at first with samurai themes. After Harunobu died in 1770, he began making prints in a similar style of life in the pleasure districts. He made about 2,500 known designs. One series of beauties ran for 140 prints, the longest known in ukiyo-e.

Leighton had family money behind him. His grandfather was the physician to two Russian tsars, and his father paid him an allowance all his life. He trained in Europe, first with Eduard von Steinle and then with Giovanni Costa. At 17 he met the philosopher Arthur Schopenhauer in Frankfurt and drew his portrait, the only known full length study of Schopenhauer done from life. From 1855 he lived in Paris for four years and met Ingres, Delacroix, Corot and Millet. His peerage was the shortest in history, because it ended with his death after one day.

Lely was born Pieter van der Faes in Soest, where his father served as an officer, and he is said to have taken the name Lely from a lily on the gable of a house in The Hague. He studied in Haarlem and became a master of the guild there in 1637. He arrived in London around 1643. After Anthony van Dyck's death he became the most fashionable portrait painter in England. His career survived Charles I's execution, and he painted Oliver Cromwell warts and all. In 1661 Charles II named him his Principal Painter in Ordinary.

Claude was born in the Duchy of Lorraine, but he spent most of his life in Italy. He is one of the earliest artists in the west to concentrate on landscape. He often added a few small figures to a landscape, so that it passed as a history painting of a Bible or classical scene. He brought the sun and streaming sunlight into many paintings, which had been rare before. Over time his landscapes grew larger, with fewer figures, and he painted them more carefully and at a slower rate. English collectors loved his work after his death.

Roghman was the son of an engraver, his mother came from the Savery family, and he studied with his great uncle and namesake, Roelant Savery. Houbraken says he had only one eye but still painted in a rough and ready way. He specialized in landscapes, and he followed Rembrandt and Hercules Seghers. With his sister Geertruydt he worked on a series of more than 200 prints of castles and country estates in North Holland and Utrecht, which proved very popular. He never married and died in the old men's almshouse in Amsterdam.

Quellinus came from a family of sculptors and painters, and his brother was the sculptor Artus Quellinus the Elder. His engravings after Artus helped spread the Flemish Baroque style across Europe. In 1650 he went to Rome and joined the Bentvueghels. His nickname there was Saracin. By 1660 he was in Amsterdam, working on a publication about the new City Hall, and six years later he sold Frederik de Wit 113 copper plates for it, with the 15 year patent. He was mainly an engraver of architecture.

Simpson grew up poor in Glasgow, with a father who was a shipyard labourer and a drunk. At fourteen he was an apprentice in a lithographic firm, and later he was bound for seven years to another one. In his time off he sketched from nature and went to evening lectures on science and engineering. He left for London in 1851 and took a job with the lithographers Day and Son. When the Crimean War began, the firm Colnaghi asked him to go to the Crimea and sketch for them. He was struck by the plight of the common soldiers. He became a special artist for the Illustrated London News.
